clue.text: Steeped in alcohol gang with time imbibed, dispensing with corks?

indicators.note: what is imbibed is swallowed and so ends up inside the drinker, here the word for steeped

blocks.note: sopped means soaked, here in drink
a crew is a gang of workers
T is the standard abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: A drinker is soaked in booze and their gang has been drinking, uncorking bottle after bottle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Steeped in alcohol' looks like the definition, but it is wordplay that swallows the gang and the time. The question mark flags a definition by example: a bottle with a threaded cap needs no cork.
explanation.definitionFit: A bottle closed with a threaded cap has no need of a cork, so a screwtopped one does without corks.

clue.text: Devours seconds, and same again, having entered eaterie

indicators.note: the eatery has gone in between them, so it sits inside the pair

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for second
a caff is a cheap café, British slang
another S, the same letter again

explanation.surface: Someone goes into a cheap café and wolfs down second helpings, then more.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface makes 'seconds' a second helping of food; it is just the abbreviation S, twice. Scaff is Scots for eating greedily.
explanation.definitionFit: To scaff, in Scots, is to eat greedily or scrounge food, so scaffs means wolfs or devours.

clue.text: Game I played with CO — not one for the men

indicators.note: the letters are played about with, moved around into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written; the surface makes it a commanding officer

explanation.surface: A soldier recalls a game played with the commanding officer, though it was not meant for the ranks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Game' is fodder here, not the definition, though it tells you the answer is a sport. Camogie is the Irish women's version of hurling.
explanation.definitionFit: Camogie is played only by women, so it is a game not for the men, who play hurling instead.

clue.text: Detective — were we lost with one, missing Yard?

blocks.clueFragment: were we lost with one, missing Yard?
blocks.note: surface reading: a worried question about being left with a detective who is not from Scotland Yard

blocks.clueFragment: were we lost with one, missing Yard?
blocks.note: setter's reading: the detective's name is also a picture puzzle, the kind that leaves solvers lost, and he works in Scotland, not at the Yard

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether they would be lost with a detective who isn't from Scotland Yard.
explanation.walkthrough: Inspector Rebus is Ian Rankin's Edinburgh detective, outside Scotland Yard, the London police headquarters; a rebus is also a puzzle of pictures and letters that can leave you lost.
explanation.definitionFit: John Rebus is the fictional Edinburgh police inspector of Ian Rankin's crime novels, so a famous detective.

clue.text: How a restaurant stores such produce

indicators.note: the words before it store the letters, keeping them inside

blocks.note: the letters run on from the end of the first word, through the second, into the third

explanation.surface: A question about how a restaurant keeps its produce.
explanation.walkthrough: The hidden letters begin with the last letter of How and end three letters into restaurant.
explanation.definitionFit: Wares are goods offered for sale, and produce is goods grown or made to be sold.

clue.text: Typical of a flightless insect — hurts you badly, hospital admitted

indicators.note: badly means done wrong, so the letters come out in a scrambled order
a patient admitted is taken in, so the hospital goes inside the other letters

blocks.note: taken as written
a san is short for sanatorium, a hospital

explanation.surface: A wingless bug's sting hurts you so badly that you end up in hospital.
explanation.walkthrough: SAN goes in after the third letter of the rearranged eight. The Thysanura are the bristletails, which include the silverfish.
explanation.definitionFit: Thysanurous describes the Thysanura, primitive wingless insects such as silverfish, so typical of an insect that cannot fly.

clue.text: A spoilsport

blocks.note: read plainly: someone who spoils others' fun
the setter's reading is the same: this is a bare definition with no wordplay

explanation.walkthrough: This is Azed's competition word: it is given only a plain definition, and readers send in their own cryptic clues for it, so there is no wordplay to find.
explanation.definitionFit: A party pooper is a person who dampens the fun of others, an informal synonym for a killjoy.

clue.text: Espy deer's end, butchered — it signals culmination of hunt

indicators.note: the end of the word is its final letter
something butchered is cut up and rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
the last letter of deer

explanation.surface: A hunter spots a deer, which is then cut up as the hunt reaches its end.
explanation.walkthrough: Pryse, or prise, is an old hunting term for the horn call sounded when the quarry is taken.
explanation.definitionFit: The pryse was the note blown on a hunting horn at the capture of the beast, so the signal that the hunt has climaxed.

clue.text: They're probably not in the programme or in scene changing

definitions.text: They're probably not in the programme

indicators.note: the letters are changing places into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Items left out of a theatre's printed programme, or bits added in a scene change.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' only joins the pieces; the theatrical surface hides that 'or' is fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Encores are extra pieces played at the audience's demand after the advertised music, so normally absent from the printed programme.

clue.text: Where punters enjoy themselves? Emergency if credit is denied

indicators.note: what is denied is refused entry, so those letters are kept out

blocks.note: a crisis is an emergency
CR is the bookkeeping abbreviation for credit

explanation.surface: Gamblers enjoying themselves face an emergency if they're refused credit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Punters' suggests gamblers, but here they are people propelling flat boats with a pole. The Isis is the stretch of the Thames at Oxford, famous for punting.
explanation.definitionFit: The Isis is the river at Oxford where students take punts out for pleasure.

clue.text: Firework spent after soaring

indicators.note: soaring means going upward, and in a down entry that reads the word from bottom to top

blocks.note: to have spent one's days somewhere is to have lived there

explanation.surface: A firework is used up after it shoots skyward.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures a rocket burning out, but 'spent' is a past verb, not 'used up'.
explanation.definitionFit: A devil is a small firework that fizzes and jumps, a term recorded in Chambers.

clue.text: Scotsman's drive one from behind pouches (blind)

indicators.note: reading a word from behind means starting at its last letter and working back

blocks.note: ca' is Scots for to drive, as in driving cattle
an ace is the one in a suit of cards

explanation.surface: A Scot drives someone from behind the blinds, with pouches thrown in for no clear reason.
explanation.walkthrough: CA + ECA gives CAECA. The bracketed 'blind' belongs to the definition: anatomy calls a pouch closed at one end a blind gut.
explanation.definitionFit: Caeca is the plural of caecum, the closed-ended sac of the gut, a pouch that leads nowhere, which is why it is called blind.

clue.text: Fleshy hooter (might one jokingly suppose?)

blocks.note: first meaning: made of flesh, with a meaty texture
second meaning, a playful one: split the word into a vehicle and a nose and it becomes a name for a horn

explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a fleshy nose, since hooter is slang for nose. The second definition is a pun: CAR NOSE would be a car's hooter, the British word for its horn, and the bracket admits the joke.
explanation.definitionFit: Carnose is a botanical and zoological term meaning of flesh or with a fleshy texture, from Latin caro, carnis.

clue.text: Sort of resinous fragment of eolith kept in dresser

indicators.note: only a small fragment of the word is wanted, its opening letter
something kept in a piece of furniture sits inside it

blocks.note: an ambry is a cupboard or dresser, also a church recess for sacred vessels
the first letter of eolith

explanation.surface: A chip of an ancient flint tool, an eolith, is stored in a dresser, oddly resinous.
explanation.walkthrough: An eolith is a crudely chipped flint once taken for an early human tool; only its first letter is used. Ambry is an old word for a cupboard.
explanation.definitionFit: Ambery means like amber, which is fossilised tree resin, so it is one kind of resinous.

clue.text: Look round carriage with lots of thongs

indicators.note: round means going about the outside, so the look wraps the carriage

blocks.note: to spy is to look
a trap is a light two-wheeled horse carriage

explanation.surface: Someone peers round a carriage packed with leather thongs.
explanation.walkthrough: Thongs here are narrow strips of leather, as on sandals or a dress, not the underwear or flip-flops a modern reader may think of.
explanation.definitionFit: Strappy describes shoes or clothes made with many narrow straps, and a thong is a narrow strap.

clue.text: Knife knights collectively shortened by half

indicators.note: cutting a word down by half keeps its front half and drops the rest

blocks.note: chivalry is knights as a body, as well as their code of honour

explanation.surface: A knife belonging to an order of knights, cut down to half size.
explanation.walkthrough: The eight-letter word loses its last four letters, ALRY.
explanation.definitionFit: Chiv is slang, originally Romani, for a knife or blade, especially one used as a weapon.

clue.text: Most squalid Glaswegian drunk to tend (old)

blocks.note: fou is Scots for drunk
lest is an old form of list, to listen or attend, and tend once meant to attend

explanation.surface: A drunk in Glasgow lives in the dirtiest conditions, with an old carer looking after him.
explanation.walkthrough: The bracketed 'old' marks an obsolete word: tend here is an old sense meaning to listen, and lest is a Spenserian spelling of list with that meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: Foul means filthy or disgusting, so its superlative describes the dirtiest, most squalid conditions.

clue.text: Young thug is rarely flung around

indicators.note: turned around, the whole string reads from right to left

blocks.note: taken as written
tost is a rare old spelling of tossed, meaning flung

explanation.surface: A young thug who is seldom thrown about by anyone.
explanation.walkthrough: IS + TOST read backwards is TSOTSI. 'Rarely' is not an indicator: it warns that the spelling is a rare one.
explanation.definitionFit: Tsotsi is South African slang for a young township gangster or hoodlum.

clue.text: Mousetrap play's heroine in constant run

indicators.note: in puts the heroine inside the remaining letters

blocks.note: c is the physicist's symbol for a constant, the speed of light
Hedda Gabler is the heroine of Ibsen's play
R is the cricket scorer's abbreviation for run

explanation.surface: The heroine of The Mousetrap, the long-running Agatha Christie play, with a cast that never changes.
explanation.walkthrough: The Mousetrap is Christie's play, still running in London since 1952, so 'play' seems to point there; instead, mousetrap is slang for a cheap cheese, as used to bait traps.
explanation.definitionFit: Mousetrap is British slang for inferior cheese, especially cheddar, of the kind put in mousetraps as bait.

clue.text: Treacly cookie? Wise up, this could be rendered yellower with sirup

indicators.note: rendered here means turned into something else, so the letters are reshaped into a new word

blocks.note: the first word of the target phrase
the second word of the target phrase, an old spelling of syrup
these letters, together with the answer, make up the target phrase, so they are taken away
stands for the answer itself

explanation.surface: A sticky biscuit gets a sweeter, yellower glaze when brushed with syrup.
explanation.walkthrough: A composite anagram: the answer plus WISE UP could be rearranged into YELLOWER SIRUP, so remove WISE UP from those thirteen letters and rearrange the seven left over.
explanation.definitionFit: A rye roll is a thin crisp biscuit made with treacle or syrup, so a sticky treacly cookie.

clue.text: Gaps not applicable when filling in a clue solved

indicators.note: filling something in puts material inside its holes
a solved puzzle has been worked out, so the letters are worked into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
N/A is the form-filling abbreviation for not applicable

explanation.surface: A note on gaps in a form that do not apply when the solver is filling in a puzzle.
explanation.walkthrough: The rearranged A CLUE takes NA before its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Lacunae are gaps or missing parts, especially in a text or argument; it is the Latin plural of lacuna.

clue.text: Like a flea or hopper (an ant is different)

indicators.note: the letters are made different, rearranged into another order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Describing jumping insects, a flea or grasshopper, while noting that an ant is not one of them.
explanation.walkthrough: The bracket hides the anagram indicator in an aside, so the clue reads like a zoology note. Siphonaptera is the insect order of fleas.
explanation.definitionFit: Siphonapteran describes a member of the Siphonaptera, the order of wingless blood-sucking insects that contains the fleas.

clue.text: Teachers with young trouble-maker given painful confrontation with head?

blocks.note: the NUT was the National Union of Teachers
a Ted, or Teddy boy, was a 1950s British youth tearaway

explanation.surface: Teachers facing a young troublemaker end up having a painful meeting with the head teacher.
explanation.walkthrough: The head looks like the head teacher, but it is the one on someone's shoulders, used as a weapon.
explanation.definitionFit: To nut someone is British slang for to headbutt them, a painful meeting with someone's forehead.

clue.text: Dupe's misled about former flame getting turned on

indicators.note: something misled is sent the wrong way, so its letters go astray into a new order
about means around, so these letters wrap round the next piece

blocks.note: taken as written, the apostrophe ignored
an ex is a former partner

explanation.surface: A gullible person is led astray when an old lover reappears and things heat up.
explanation.walkthrough: The rearranged letters go round EX after their first letter S.
explanation.definitionFit: Sexed up is slang for sexually aroused, the same idea as being turned on.

clue.text: Young fish, second caught with perch

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for second
c is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for caught
a perch, rod or pole is an old unit of length

explanation.surface: An angler catches a young fish and a perch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perch' looks like a second fish but is the old measure of five and a half yards.
explanation.definitionFit: A scrod is a young cod or haddock, especially one split and prepared for cooking in New England.

clue.text: Spenser's to work at being a poet

blocks.note: first meaning: Spenser's old infinitive form of to do
second meaning: the metaphysical poet, author of the Holy Sonnets

explanation.walkthrough: Spenser, the Elizabethan poet of The Faerie Queene, used archaic forms that Chambers records with his name; this one is a form of the verb do, to work at.
explanation.definitionFit: John Donne (1572-1631) was the English metaphysical poet, and Spenser wrote donne for the infinitive do.

clue.text: Strangely blue about start of gestation? It'll show then

indicators.note: strangely means oddly, so the letters come out in an odd order
the start of a word is its first letter
about means around, so the rearranged letters surround the next piece

blocks.note: taken as written
the first letter of gestation

explanation.surface: Feeling oddly down at the start of a pregnancy, before it starts to show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Then' points back to the gestation: once a pregnancy is under way, a swelling becomes visible.
explanation.definitionFit: A pregnant woman's bulge is the swelling of her belly, which is what shows as the pregnancy advances.

clue.text: Subjects for meditation yielding reverse of satisfactory answer

indicators.note: the reverse of a word is that word written backwards

blocks.note: OK means satisfactory
ans. is the abbreviation for answer

explanation.surface: Topics to meditate on that produce the opposite of a satisfying answer.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface fits the subject: a Zen koan is meant to defeat a logical answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Koans are paradoxical riddles that Zen Buddhist teachers set pupils to meditate on.

clue.text: Cover for tomb held in much adoration

indicators.note: the letters are held inside the following words, running across the space between them

blocks.note: the letters run on from the end of the first word into the start of the second

explanation.surface: A cloth laid over a grave in deep reverence.
explanation.walkthrough: Most solvers know the word as a woman's veil, but the chador or chadar is also the cloth spread over a revered tomb.
explanation.definitionFit: A chador, also spelt chadar, is a large sheet of cloth, worn as a veil or spread as a covering over a tomb.

clue.text: What limits human? It may be a bit of a dilemma

indicators.note: what limits something hems it in on both sides, so these end letters enclose the rest

blocks.note: the first and last letters of human, its limits
something that may be one thing or another is offered with this word of alternatives

explanation.surface: Asking what restricts a person, and suggesting it might be a small dilemma.
explanation.walkthrough: A dilemma is traditionally pictured as a beast with two horns, so each of the two unpleasant choices is one part of it.
explanation.definitionFit: To be on the horns of a dilemma is to face two bad choices, each choice being one horn.

clue.text: Treat for wedding bairns, grub after turning up with nothing inside

indicators.note: turning a word reverses its direction
inside puts the nothing within the turned word
after sends the grub to the back, though the clue names it first

blocks.note: taken as written, then turned round
O looks like zero, nothing
to rout is to root or grub about, as a pig does

explanation.surface: Food served to children at a wedding, made from turned-up grub with nothing in it.
explanation.walkthrough: Bairns are children in Scots. A pour-out is the Scottish custom of the bridal party throwing coins for children to scramble for after a wedding.
explanation.definitionFit: The pour-out is the shower of coins thrown at a Scottish wedding, a treat the local children scramble to collect.

clue.text: Course followed by crew? Sounds like it

indicators.note: the clue says the answer only sounds like the phrase before it

blocks.note: a course followed by a rowing crew is one they have rowed

explanation.surface: Asking whether a crew follows the course, then answering that it sounds right.
explanation.walkthrough: A rowing crew rows its course, and a course that has been rowed is pronounced exactly like a road.
explanation.definitionFit: A road is a route or way, which is one meaning of course, the way taken from one place to another.

clue.text: I put in something for the garden that's easy to train?

indicators.note: a thing put in another goes inside it

blocks.note: a plant is what a gardener puts in the ground
taken as written

explanation.surface: A gardener plants something that will be easy to train up a trellis.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface sounds like training a climbing plant, which is how the question mark earns its place: a pliant stem trains easily, and so does a pliant person.
explanation.definitionFit: Pliant means bending readily, so flexible and yielding, and something yielding is easy to shape or teach.

clue.text: Nothing jolly about a gun going off? Method of investigation required

indicators.note: about means around, so the marine wraps round the following letters
a gun going off is a disturbance, so its letters are thrown into a new order

blocks.note: O looks like zero, nothing
a jolly is slang for a Royal Marine, RM
taken as written

explanation.surface: A gun going off near a cheerful man is no fun, so someone has to investigate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jolly' looks like an adjective but is old naval slang for a Royal Marine.
explanation.definitionFit: Organum, like organon, is a system of logical rules for reasoning, the name of works by Aristotle and Bacon on scientific inquiry.

clue.text: Hospital dept? Some taken in, say, after a turn

indicators.note: taken in means received inside something else
after a turn the assembled letters face the other way

blocks.note: e.g., for example, is the abbreviation for say
any and some are interchangeable in many sentences

explanation.surface: A hospital department where patients are admitted after a funny turn.
explanation.walkthrough: ANY goes between the E and G, then the whole is read backwards. Gynae is short for gynaecology, the medical specialty of women's reproductive health.
explanation.definitionFit: Gynae is British shorthand for a hospital's gynaecology department or ward.

clue.text: In a hurry instals reserve fund, not reinforced

definitions.note: in building, prestressed concrete is set apart from ordinary reinforced concrete, which is the contrast this definition leans on

indicators.note: to install a thing is to set it in place inside something else

blocks.note: pressed for time means in a hurry
the rest is a bank's reserve fund

explanation.surface: Someone in a rush sets up an emergency fund without backing it properly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rest' as a reserve fund is the banking sense, the surplus held back by the Bank of England. The reserve goes in right after the first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Prestressed concrete is strengthened by steel tensioned before loading, a technique engineers distinguish from conventional reinforcement with passive steel bars.
